summary: An April Fools' RFC that jokingly proposes to boost IPv6 by turning social networking platforms into IPv6 networks, instantly adding millions of hosts. It is humor and not a real protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This is an April 1st joke document proposing IPv6 over social networks. It describes users as routers and their connections as links, with packets moving only when users trigger processing.

subtitle: An April 1st joke about carrying IPv6 packets through social networks.

tldr.problem: The RFC jokes that IPv6 use could be increased by treating social networking platforms as IPv6 networks.
tldr.mechanism: It imagines each user as a router and each friendship as a point-to-point link, with the account owner manually triggering packet processing.
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1st Experimental joke RFC. The text also describes a prototype and reports its measured operation in March 2009.

today: RFC 5514 is Experimental and dated April 1, 2009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The April 1st Proposal
sections.content: RFC 5514 is an April 1st joke document that proposes turning social networking platforms into IPv6 networks. It describes each user as a router with a loopback interface and each connection between users as a point-to-point link. Social network applications could generate IPv6 packets on a user's behalf.
sections.plainLanguage: This April 1st joke treats social network users as IPv6 routers. A connection between two users becomes a link for packets.

sections.title: Addressing and Packet Processing
sections.content: The RFC assigns each user a loopback address based on the user's numerical identification and describes a link-local address formed using the same identifier. Because an account owner must explicitly trigger IPv6 processing, packets move from user to user only when people activate the application. The RFC says this creates high latency and recommends UDP rather than TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal builds addresses from each user's account identification. Packets wait for account owners to trigger processing, so delays can be very long.

sections.title: The Reported Prototype
sections.content: The RFC says the author developed a working prototype using Facebook and reports figures from March 26, 2009. It lists a packet rate of 160 packets per minute and 3,800 nodes. The text includes an example ping sent on February 24, 2009, with a reply received on February 26, illustrating the delay described by the proposal.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC reports a prototype with 3,800 nodes. Its example ping took from February 24 to February 26 to receive a reply.
